title: The Single-Base 0/1 Predicate
content: `ZeroOne d a := (Nat.digits d a).toFinset ⊆ {0,1}` is exactly the per-base condition used in the parent theorem `Erdos124.erdos_conjecture_true`, here applied to one base. The helper `mem_zeroOne_iff` records the trivial but repeatedly used fact that a digit lies in `{0,1}` iff it is `< 2`. At `k = 1` the parent's representation `n = ∑ᵢ aᵢ` forces `a = n`, so 'base `d` is complete' means precisely that every `n` already satisfies `ZeroOne d n`.
mathContext: A digit system in base $d$ uses digits $0, 1, \dots, d-1$. Restricting to digits $\{0,1\}$ keeps only the 'subset-sum of distinct powers of $d$' numbers; for these to exhaust ℕ is a strong constraint on $d$.

title: Sufficiency: Base 2 Is Always 0/1
content: `zeroOne_base_two` is the positive half: every natural number is 0/1-representable in base 2, because each binary digit is `< 2` (`Nat.digits_lt_base` with `2 ≤ 2`). This is the `k = 1, d = 2` instance of the parent's completeness theorem and supplies the reverse direction of the characterisation.
mathContext: Binary representation: every $n$ has digits in $\{0,1\}$ in base $2$, equivalently $n$ is a sum of distinct powers of $2$.

title: The Explicit Obstruction: the Number 2
content: `digits_two_of_three_le` computes `Nat.digits d 2 = [2]` for every `d ≥ 3` (via `Nat.digits_def'`, since `2 % d = 2` and `2 / d = 0`). Then `not_zeroOne_two_of_three_le` concludes `¬ ZeroOne d 2`: the only digit of `2` is `2 ∉ {0,1}`. A single smallest non-trivial number already breaks completeness the moment the base exceeds 2 — no asymptotics required.
mathContext: For $0 < a < d$ the base-$d$ representation of $a$ is the single digit $[a]$. With $a = 2$ and $d \ge 3$ this digit is $2$, which is forbidden in a $\{0,1\}$ system.

title: Completeness ⇔ d = 2
content: `zeroOne_all_iff_two`: for a single base `d ≥ 2`, every natural number is 0/1-representable in base `d` iff `d = 2`. Forward is the contrapositive using the `n = 2` obstruction (any `d ≥ 3` fails); reverse is base-2 completeness. This isolates `d = 2` as the unique complete single base.
mathContext: Among all bases, base $2$ is the unique one whose digit alphabet is already $\{0,1\}$, so it is the only single base for which the $0/1$ restriction is vacuous.

title: The Erdős Threshold at k = 1
content: `sum_cond_iff_two`: at a single base the Erdős sum `∑ᵢ 1/(dᵢ−1)` is just `1/(d−1)`, and the threshold `1 ≤ 1/(d−1)` holds iff `d = 2` (for `d ≥ 2`). Proved by clearing the positive denominator with `le_div_iff₀` and elementary casting. This is the arithmetic side of the boundary that must match the digit side.
mathContext: $1/(d-1) \ge 1 \iff d - 1 \le 1 \iff d \le 2$, so among $d \ge 2$ only $d = 2$ meets the Erdős threshold.

title: Sharpness: Necessary and Sufficient at the Boundary
content: `single_base_complete_iff_sum_cond` chains the two equivalences: for `d ≥ 2`, completeness `(∀ n, ZeroOne d n)` holds iff `1 ≤ 1/(d−1)`. So the parent's condition, proved only *sufficient* there, is at the single-base boundary *necessary and sufficient*. This is the converse the parent leaves open in the `k = 1` case, and the headline result of the entry.
mathContext: A sufficient condition is sharp at a boundary when its failure provably destroys the conclusion. Here the boundary is $k = 1$, where the Erdős inequality is exactly the dividing line $d = 2$ vs $d \ge 3$.
